A theremin is a musical instrument — specifically, an electronic musical instrument — and it holds a remarkable distinction: it is one of the very few instruments in the world that you play without touching it at all.

A theremin is a box-shaped device, roughly the size of a small suitcase, that sits on a stand. Sticking out of it are two metal antennas:

  • A straight vertical rod on the right side
  • A horizontal loop (like a sideways horseshoe) on the left side

That's it. No strings, no keys, no buttons.

The performer stands in front of the theremin and moves their bare hands through the air near these two antennas — never touching them.

  • The right hand, moved closer to or farther from the vertical rod, controls pitch (how high or low the note sounds). Moving the hand closer raises the pitch; moving it away lowers it.
  • The left hand, moved closer to or farther from the horizontal loop, controls volume (how loud or soft the sound is). Moving the hand closer makes the sound quieter; moving it away makes it louder.

So a theremin player essentially sculpts invisible sound in the air using only the movement of their hands. There is nothing to press, pluck, or bow. The instrument senses the position of the human body through electromagnetic fields — invisible zones of energy that surround the antennas. When a hand enters that zone, it disturbs the field, and the instrument converts that disturbance into sound through a speaker.

The theremin produces a continuous, smooth, eerie, and hauntingly beautiful tone — often described as resembling a human singing voice, or something like a cello or violin, but with an otherworldly, ghostly quality. Because the pitch changes in a completely smooth, unbroken glide (there are no frets or keys to create distinct "steps"), the sound flows like a voice sliding between notes.

This gives the theremin its signature character: it sounds deeply expressive and slightly unsettling at the same time — human-like, yet not quite human.
Why It Is So Difficult to Play

Because there are no physical reference points — no keys to feel under your fingers, no strings to press — the theremin player has nothing to guide their hands except their own ear and muscle memory. Moving a finger even a few centimetres in the wrong direction produces the wrong note. Achieving precise pitch requires extraordinary control and practice, which is why skilled theremin players are relatively rare.

Even if you didn't know the word, you have almost certainly heard a theremin before. Its eerie sound became hugely popular in science fiction and horror films from the mid-20th century onward. Whenever you hear that ghostly, wavering "woooo" sound in an old horror or alien movie, that is often a theremin.

It also appears in well-known popular music. The Beach Boys used it famously in their 1966 hit Good Vibrations. It has been used in classical compositions, film scores, and experimental music across many decades.

The theremin was invented around 1920, making it one of the earliest electronic instruments ever created — predating the synthesizer by decades. This makes it historically significant: it was a pioneer of the idea that electricity itself could be used to make music, not just amplify it.
The Word Used in a Sentence

• "She played a haunting melody on the theremin without once touching the instrument."
  • "The eerie sound in that old horror movie was produced by a theremin."
  • "Learning the theremin is notoriously difficult because there are no physical keys or strings to guide the player."

A theremin is an early electronic musical instrument played by moving your hands through the air near its antennas, without any physical contact. It produces a smooth, eerie, voice-like sound, and is controlled entirely through invisible electromagnetic fields. It is one of the oldest electronic instruments ever made, and its ghostly tone has made it iconic in horror films, science fiction, and experimental music.
